newsitem.title: CHINA: HK needs new moves to meet housing goals - lawmaker.
newsitem.headline: HK needs new moves to meet housing goals - lawmaker.

text.p: Hong Kong will need to carry out a series of new initiatives to allow property developers to reach government housing goals and convince the market that home prices are set to moderate, a veteran legislator said on Monday.

While Hong Kong's chief executive Tung Chee-hwa has made housing a top priority, Ronald Arculli of the pro-business Liberal Party said Tung needed to initiate land planning, labour and infrastructure policy changes to meet housing targets.
"If our priorities lie in housing, there are certain things that might need innovation," Arculli, who is a spokesman for Hong Kong's Real Estate Developers Association, told Reuters.

Speeding up the conversion of land for residential use and reconsidering urban development plans and plot ratio constraints would be some of the issues the government would need to address to provide enough land, he said in an interview.

In his inaugural speech on July 1, when China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong, Tung said the government aimed to tackle exorbitant housing prices with an increase in housing supply to an annual target of 85,000 new apartments.
Since then, the government has announced a five-year land disposal programme which would boost new residential land supply by 140 percent compared with the previous five years.

The moves caused a slowdown in Hong Kong's soaring property market, where prices rose about 30 percent during the first half of the year, but Arculli said the government would have to reveal more details to moderate prices in the future.
"Say the government produces the land. Where are you going to get the labour? It is so costly that you increase the price of the product through the production costs," said Arculli.
"Part of the problems that the new administration will have to tackle will in fact be to have a scheme for the importation of labour," he said.
The Real Estate Developers Association (REDA) has also been pushing the government to allow the private sector to develop the infrastructure required for new residential zones.

"What the government has always done is to say, 'We can't give you the land until the infrastructure is in place'," said Arculli. "REDA has always said, "You have constraints on your capacity, let us the private developers handle it".
While the government has spoken about this in the past, nothing had actually been done, Arculli added.
Tung is due to deliver a policy statement in October which is expected to detail the government's housing plans.
While supply side measures are likely to be the main thrust of the government's new housing policy, Tung has said he would launch punitive measures against speculators if necessary.
But Arculli said the best way to stamp out speculation would be to convince the market that supply targets would be met and housing price rises would subsequently moderate.
"It is a question of the public believing that Mr Tung will live up to his commitment and that the developers can deliver and will deliver."

"The developers have always said that in terms of excessive speculation, the free market will sooner or later even things out. What developers want is for business people to make business decisions and not government officials to make business decisions," Arculli said.
